sentences.text: His grandmother had told him, once, that you could send a note up a kite string.

She had told him in the front room in the winter, when he was small enough to be on the floor, and she had described it exactly: you write it on a scrap, you make a ring of it round the string, and you let it go, and the wind walks it up.
All the way to the top.
She said her brother had done it in Aberdaron in about 1951 and that it had taken most of an afternoon.
He had never had a kite that stayed up long enough to try.
He had the pen in his pocket already, which tells you something about what he had been hoping for.
He wrote it on the back of a bus ticket, holding the string under his arm, with the paper against his knee.
It was not a wish.
He wants that understood, because people always assume it was a wish, and there is something a bit cheap about a wish.
It was four words about his grandmother.
They are his, and he has never told anyone what they were, including the two people who have asked properly.
He curled the ticket into a ring and hooked it over the string and let go.
It went up in little hops.
That was the part nobody had described to him.
It did not travel smoothly; it caught, and stuck, and shivered, and then a gust would come along the line and it would run four or five metres and catch again.
He stood with his head back and his neck aching and watched a bus ticket climb a piece of string for thirteen minutes.
He lost sight of it twice and found it again both times.
When it reached the kite — when it finally got up to where the string met the bridle, so far away that it was only a change in the shape of the thing — the crows let go.
All seven, at once, from the wire, and they did not fly.
They simply dropped forward off the line and opened out and were gone in seven directions, low, over the hedge and the church and the allotments.
And the kite went on flying.
For about four seconds, with nothing holding the line and nobody pulling, in air that had gone completely still, the kite stayed exactly where it was.
Then it came down.

It came down slowly and in a long slant, across the field, over the wall, into the long grass by the water trough where the nettles are, and Dai walked the whole length of the field to get it with the slack string looping along the ground behind him.
It was not damaged.
One spar had come out of its pocket, which took a minute to fix.
The ticket was gone.
He looked for it.
He looked properly, for about half an hour, on his hands and knees in the long grass, and it was not there, and the string was unbroken from his hand to the bridle with nothing on it.
He flew that kite for four more summers.
It is in his loft now, in a bag, with the envelope.
He never sent another one.
